stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
Crack Closure in Mortar Samples after 28 Days (% of crack width sealed)
Mortar type | 50% humidity | 95% humidity
Plain | 12 | 18
With bacterial spores | 15 | 71

Some engineers mix dormant bacterial spores into mortar so that the material can repair itself. When water seeps into a fresh crack, it revives the spores. The spores then turn a calcium-based nutrient packed into the mortar into calcite, which gradually fills the gap. Materials scientist Leilani Kahale and her colleagues compared plain mortar with spore-treated mortar at two humidity levels. They concluded that the advantage the spores provide depends heavily on available moisture: for example, ______
choices: at 95% humidity, mortar with spores sealed 71% of its crack width, whereas plain mortar sealed only 18%.
the spores raised crack closure by 53 percentage points at 95% humidity but by only 3 points at 50% humidity.
plain mortar sealed a larger share of its crack width at 95% humidity than it did at 50% humidity.
at 50% humidity, mortar with spores sealed a smaller share of its crack width than plain mortar did.
explanation: The claim is about the spores' advantage, meaning how much better spore-treated mortar does than plain mortar, and says that this advantage changes with moisture. To show it, you need the gap between the two mortar types at both humidity levels. At 95% humidity the gap is 71 − 18 = 53 points. At 50% humidity it is 15 − 12 = 3 points. Choice B gives both gaps, so it shows that the advantage is large when moisture is plentiful and nearly disappears when it is scarce.

A.why: This is an accurate reading of the table, but it covers only the high-humidity condition. It shows that the spores help when moisture is plentiful, but the claim is that their advantage depends on moisture. You can't show dependence without comparing the advantage across both humidity levels. You picked a true statement that doesn't prove the passage's point.

C.why: This is true (18% versus 12%), but it describes only plain mortar, which has no spores. The claim is about what the spores add, so a choice that leaves out the spore-treated samples can't support it. You matched the topic of moisture instead of the specific claim.

D.why: This misreads the table. At 50% humidity, mortar with spores sealed 15% of its crack width and plain mortar sealed 12%, so the spore-treated mortar did slightly better, not worse. Check the direction of each comparison against the numbers.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
Raccoons climb the poles of nest boxes to take eggs and chicks, and a metal cone guard fixed to the pole stops the climb. Ornithologist Priya Raman put guards on half the tree swallow boxes at each of three sites. Raccoons were common only at the marsh edge. She concluded that guards substantially improve fledging success only where climbing predators are abundant. For example, guarded boxes ______

Tree Swallow Fledging Success (% of eggs producing fledglings)
Site | Unguarded boxes | Guarded boxes
Marsh edge | 41 | 78
Meadow | 62 | 66
Orchard | 58 | 61
choices: had fledging success above 60% at all three sites, including the orchard.
beat unguarded boxes by 37 percentage points at the marsh edge but by only 4 at the meadow.
had higher fledging success at the meadow than they had at the marsh edge.
beat unguarded boxes by 3 percentage points at the orchard, 1 point less than at the meadow.
explanation: Raman's claim has a scope limit: guards help a lot *only where* predators are common. To show that, you have to set the raccoon site against a site with few raccoons. At the marsh edge, guards raised success from 41% to 78%, a gain of 37 points. At the meadow, the gain was 66 − 62 = 4 points. That contrast is exactly what the claim describes.

A.why: This is true, since 78, 66 and 61 are all above 60. But it describes guarded boxes alone. It never compares them with unguarded boxes, and it doesn't separate the high-predator site from the others, so it can't show that the benefit depends on predators.

C.why: You misread the table. Guarded boxes reached 78% at the marsh edge and only 66% at the meadow, so the comparison runs the other way.

D.why: This is the subtype's trap. The numbers are right (61 − 58 = 3 and 66 − 62 = 4), but both sites had few raccoons. Comparing two low-predator sites can't show that guards matter where predators are common.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
stimulus:
Concrete hardens through hydration, a reaction between cement and water, and that reaction slows sharply in cold weather. Because hydration continues for weeks, though, engineers at a state road agency argue that cold curing delays strength gain without greatly reducing the strength concrete eventually reaches. In tests on cylinders cast from a single batch, those cured at 5°C ______

Compressive Strength of Test Cylinders (MPa)
Curing temperature | Day 7 | Day 28
5°C | 18 | 39
20°C | 29 | 41
choices: were 11 MPa weaker than 20°C cylinders at day 7 but only 2 MPa weaker at day 28.
were weaker than 20°C cylinders at day 7 and stayed weaker than them at day 28.
were stronger than 20°C cylinders at day 28 despite being weaker at day 7.
matched 20°C cylinders at day 28, showing that cold has no effect on final strength.
explanation: The claim has two parts: cold *delays* strength gain, and it does *not greatly reduce* final strength. The data has to show a large early gap that nearly closes. At day 7 the gap is 29 − 18 = 11 MPa, and at day 28 it is 41 − 39 = 2 MPa. Only this choice shows both parts.

B.why: This is accurate, but it leaves out how big the gaps are. Without that, it can't show the gap shrinking. Read alone, "stayed weaker" even points away from the claim that final strength is barely reduced.

C.why: At day 28 the 5°C cylinders reached 39 MPa and the 20°C cylinders reached 41 MPa, so the cold-cured cylinders were still weaker. You reversed the comparison.

D.why: The values are 39 and 41, so they don't match. The claim also says cold doesn't *greatly* reduce final strength, not that it has *no* effect. This choice states a stronger claim than either the engineers or the table support.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the example?
stimulus: Lake-effect snow forms when cold air crosses open water, gathers moisture and drops it as snow once it reaches land. Over Lake Merrin, winter winds blow almost always from west to east. Westport sits on the lake's western shore and Easton on its eastern shore. Alder and Kell lie 30 kilometers inland, to the west and east. A regional climatologist concludes that the lake's downwind shore receives far heavier snowfall than its upwind shore. For example, ______

figure.caption: Average Annual Snowfall at Four Stations near Lake Merrin
figure.alt: Bar graph of average annual snowfall in centimeters at four stations: Alder, Westport, Easton and Kell.

choices: Easton averaged 60 cm more snow per year than Kell, which also lies east of the lake.
Westport averaged 20 cm more snow per year than Alder, which also lies west of the lake.
Easton averaged three times as much snow per year as Westport, on the opposite shore.
Kell averaged less snow per year than Westport, despite lying east of the lake.
explanation: Start with the direction. The wind blows west to east, so the eastern shore is downwind and the western shore is upwind. The claim compares the two shores, so you need Easton against Westport. Easton gets 240 cm and Westport gets 80 cm, three times as much. Both towns are on the shore, so the only difference between them is which side of the lake they are on.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. The reading is correct (240 − 180 = 60), but Easton and Kell are both on the downwind side. Comparing two places on the same side can't show a difference between the two sides.

B.why: This is also correct (80 − 60 = 20), but both stations are upwind, west of the lake. It tells you nothing about the downwind shore.

D.why: Kell averaged 180 cm and Westport averaged 80 cm, so Kell had more snow, not less. You misread the bar heights.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
stimulus:
In drypoint, an artist scratches lines straight into a copper plate. This throws up a ridge of metal, the burr, which holds extra ink and prints a soft, velvety line. Each pass through the press flattens the burr a little. Etched lines, bitten into the plate by acid, have no burr to lose. Conservator Ines Valdés argues that drypoint plates therefore wear out far sooner than etched ones. In her printing trial, ______

Line Detail Retained Compared with First Proof (%)
Impression | Drypoint plate | Etched plate
10th | 96 | 99
30th | 71 | 97
50th | 44 | 95
choices: both plates kept more than 90% of their line detail through the 10th impression.
the etched plate kept 99% of its line detail at the 10th impression and 97% at the 30th.
the drypoint plate kept more detail at the 50th impression than the etched plate did at the 30th.
from the 10th to the 50th impression, the drypoint plate lost 52 points of detail and the etched plate 4.
explanation: Valdés claims drypoint plates wear out *far sooner* than etched ones. To show that, you need both plates' loss over the same run of impressions. From the 10th to the 50th impression, the drypoint plate dropped from 96% to 44%, a loss of 52 points. The etched plate dropped from 99% to 95%, a loss of 4 points. That contrast is what the claim needs.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. It is true (96% and 99%), but it shows the two plates being *similar*. The claim is about how differently they wear.

B.why: The numbers are right, but they describe only the etched plate. Without the drypoint figures, there's no comparison to show which plate wears out sooner.

C.why: At the 50th impression the drypoint plate kept 44%, and at the 30th the etched plate kept 97%. The drypoint plate kept far less detail, not more.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
Adjuvants are substances added to vaccines to strengthen the immune response. To test one adjuvant, immunologist Rana Okafor gave two groups of mice the same vaccine. The doses were identical except that one group's also contained the adjuvant. She measured antibody levels in both groups two and six weeks later. Okafor concluded that the adjuvant's advantage grows over time instead of appearing only early on: for example, ______

Mean Antibody Level in Mice (units)
Week | Without adjuvant | With adjuvant
2 | 40 | 55
6 | 35 | 90
choices: in the group with the adjuvant, antibody levels rose from 55 units at week 2 to 90 units at week 6.
the adjuvant group's lead over the other group was 15 units at week 2 and 55 units at week 6.
at week 2, the adjuvant group's antibody level of 55 units exceeded the other group's level of 40 units.
in the group without the adjuvant, antibody levels rose from 35 units at week 2 to 40 units at week 6.
explanation: The claim is about the adjuvant's advantage, which is the gap between the two groups, and it says that gap grows. You need the gap at both time points. At week 2 the adjuvant group led by 15 units (55 − 40), and at week 6 it led by 55 units (90 − 35). The lead got bigger, so the advantage grew.

A.why: This is an accurate reading of the table, but it describes only one group. A rise within the adjuvant group says nothing about its advantage over the other group, because that group's levels could have risen just as much. You chose a true statement that doesn't show the point the sentence is making.

C.why: This is true, and it shows that the adjuvant helped at week 2. But the claim is that the advantage grows over time, and a single early comparison can't show growth. A choice like this is exactly what Okafor says the result is more than.

D.why: You reversed the numbers. Without the adjuvant, antibody levels went from 40 units at week 2 down to 35 units at week 6. They fell, so they didn't rise. This group's own trend is also beside the point of the claim.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the example?
stimulus: Endurance athletes lose sodium in sweat, and low blood sodium can hasten fatigue. Because athletes sweat more in heat, this loss is greatest on hot days. A team of sports scientists had cyclists ride to exhaustion in a cool room and in a hot room. The cyclists drank either plain water or an otherwise identical drink with added sodium. The team concluded that the sodium drink lessened, though it did not eliminate, the toll that heat took on endurance: for example, ______

figure.caption: Mean Riding Time to Exhaustion by Room Temperature and Drink
figure.alt: Bar graph of mean riding time to exhaustion for four conditions: cool room with water, cool room with sodium drink, hot room with water, and hot room with sodium drink.

choices: in cool conditions, cyclists rode for 60 minutes whether they drank water or the sodium drink.
with water, cyclists rode for 60 minutes in cool conditions but only 36 minutes in hot conditions.
moving from cool to hot conditions cut riding time by 24 minutes with the sodium drink but by 12 with water.
moving from cool to hot conditions cut riding time by 12 minutes with the sodium drink but by 24 with water.
explanation: First work out what the sentence needs: the drop caused by heat should be smaller with the sodium drink than with water, and it still shouldn't be zero. With water, riding time fell from 60 to 36 minutes, a loss of 24. With the sodium drink, it fell from 60 to 48 minutes, a loss of 12. The toll was smaller but still there, which matches both parts of the claim.

A.why: This is an accurate reading, but it describes only the cool room, where there is no heat to take a toll. A similarity between the drinks in cool conditions can't show that the drink reduced the effect of heat.

B.why: This is true, and it shows that heat hurts endurance. But it covers only the water condition, so it never shows that the sodium drink made the heat's toll smaller. You picked an accurate comparison that misses the point of the sentence.

C.why: You attached the numbers to the wrong drinks. The 24-minute drop happened with water (60 to 36), and the 12-minute drop happened with the sodium drink (60 to 48). As written, this choice says the drink made the heat's toll worse.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
Cooking pots absorb fats from the food prepared in them, and chemical tests on these residues can show whether a household cooked fish. Researchers tested pots from two ancient villages, one on the coast and one about 40 kilometers inland. The pots were dated to before and after a stone road was built linking the two villages. The team concluded that the road changed inland diets far more than it changed coastal ones: for example, ______

Pots with Marine Food Residue (%)
Village | Before road | After road
Coastal | 70 | 72
Inland | 8 | 41
choices: the coastal village had a larger share of pots with marine residue than the inland village had, both before and after the road.
after the road, the inland village's share of pots with marine residue, 41 percent, was still below the coastal village's share.
the share of pots with marine residue rose by 2 percentage points at the inland village but by 33 at the coastal village.
the share of pots with marine residue rose by 33 percentage points at the inland village but by only 2 at the coastal village.
explanation: The claim compares how much each village's diet changed. That means you need the change at both villages, side by side. At the inland village, the share rose from 8 to 41 percent, an increase of 33 points. At the coastal village, it rose from 70 to 72 percent, an increase of only 2 points. The inland change was far larger, which is exactly what the claim says.

A.why: This is true, but it compares the two villages at fixed points in time. It doesn't compare how much each one changed. A steady gap between the villages can't show that the road changed one diet more than the other.

B.why: This is an accurate reading, but it's a single after-road comparison between the villages. It says nothing about how much either village changed, and change is what the claim is about.

C.why: You swapped the villages. The 33-point rise was inland (8 to 41 percent), and the 2-point rise was on the coast (70 to 72 percent). As written, this choice would mean the road changed coastal diets more.

stem: Which choice does NOT effectively use data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
Sports physiologist Dana Ruel tested whether a carbohydrate drink protects cyclists against fatigue. Riders completed trials of five different lengths, drinking either a carbohydrate solution or flavored water, and then rode one all-out sprint. Ruel concluded that the drink mattered only in long efforts: in trials of 90 minutes or more, riders who had the drink lost less sprint power than riders who had water. For example, ______

Average Drop in Final Sprint Power (%)
Trial length | Water | Carbohydrate drink
30 minutes | 4 | 4
60 minutes | 7 | 7
90 minutes | 12 | 8
120 minutes | 18 | 11
150 minutes | 23 | 15
choices: in the 90-minute trials, riders lost 12% of sprint power with water but only 8% with the drink.
in the 120-minute trials, riders lost 18% of sprint power with water but only 11% with the drink.
in the 150-minute trials, riders lost 23% of sprint power with water but only 15% with the drink.
in the 60-minute trials, riders lost 7% of sprint power with water and 7% with the drink.
explanation: The example has to show a trial of 90 minutes or more in which drink riders lost less power than water riders. Choice D reads the table correctly, but it describes a 60-minute trial, which is outside the claim's scope, and it shows no difference at all. So it can't serve as an example of the drink helping. A, B and C each give a trial of at least 90 minutes in which the drink group lost less power, so each one completes the example.

A.why: You read '90 minutes or more' as 'more than 90 minutes' and dropped the 90-minute row. The claim includes 90, and at that length the drink group lost less power (8% against 12%), so A is a valid example.

B.why: You may have thought the drink had to cut the loss by half or more to count. The claim only says drink riders lost less, and 11% is less than 18%, so B works.

C.why: You may have judged the longest trial too extreme to be a fair example. Any trial of 90 minutes or more fits, and at 150 minutes the drink group lost less power (15% against 23%), so C completes the example.

stem: Which choice does NOT effectively use data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
Sea urchins can strip a kelp forest bare, but they graze less when predators are close. To test this, marine biologist Chidi Okafor kept urchins of three species in paired tanks that were identical except that one tank held water scented by a predatory crab. Okafor concluded that the scent's effect held for every species tested: within each species, urchins in scented tanks ate less kelp than urchins in unscented tanks. For example, ______

Kelp Eaten per Urchin (grams per day)
Species | Unscented tank | Scented tank
Purple urchin | 6 | 2
Red urchin | 9 | 5
Green urchin | 4 | 3
choices: purple urchins ate 6 grams of kelp per day in unscented tanks but 2 grams in scented tanks.
red urchins ate 5 grams of kelp per day in scented tanks, while purple urchins ate 6 grams in unscented tanks.
green urchins ate 4 grams of kelp per day in unscented tanks but 3 grams in scented tanks.
red urchins ate 9 grams of kelp per day in unscented tanks but 5 grams in scented tanks.
explanation: The claim compares scented and unscented tanks within one species, so a valid example has to keep the species fixed and change only the scent. Choice B gets both numbers right, but it compares red urchins in scented tanks with purple urchins in unscented tanks. Because both the species and the condition change, the comparison says nothing about the scent's effect. A, C and D each compare the same species across the two tanks and show less kelp eaten with the scent.

A.why: You may have thought the drop from 6 to 2 grams was too large to be typical and so couldn't serve as an example. The claim only needs scented-tank urchins to eat less, and purple urchins do, so A works.

C.why: You may have dismissed the green urchins' drop of 1 gram as too small to count. The claim is that urchins ate less with the scent, not that they ate much less, and 3 is less than 4, so C completes the example.

D.why: You may have read the columns in the wrong order and thought red urchins ate more in scented tanks. Red urchins ate 9 grams unscented and 5 grams scented, which is a drop, so D is a valid example.

stem: Which choice does NOT effectively use data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
Recycled polyethylene contains polymer chains that repeated melting has shortened. Shorter chains tangle with one another less, and that weaker tangling lets the plastic pull apart under smaller loads. Materials scientist Ines Varga therefore predicted that blending more recycled polyethylene into new plastic would lower the blend's tensile strength, and her tests supported the prediction. For example, ______

Properties of Polyethylene Blends
Recycled content (%) | Tensile strength (MPa) | Elongation at break (%)
0 | 30 | 12
25 | 27 | 12
50 | 23 | 15
75 | 18 | 19
choices: elongation at break held at 12% in both the 0% blend and the 25% blend.
tensile strength fell from 30 MPa in the 0% blend to 27 MPa in the 25% blend.
tensile strength fell from 27 MPa in the 25% blend to 23 MPa in the 50% blend.
tensile strength fell from 30 MPa in the 0% blend to 18 MPa in the 75% blend.
explanation: Varga predicted that more recycled content would mean lower tensile strength, so the example has to show strength falling as recycled content rises. Choice A reads the table correctly, but it describes elongation at break, which is a different property, so it says nothing about strength. B, C and D each show tensile strength dropping as recycled content goes up, and each one supports the prediction.

B.why: You may have thought a 3 MPa drop was too small to count as evidence. The prediction is about the direction of change, and strength did fall from 30 to 27 MPa as recycled content rose, so B works.

C.why: You may have thought an example had to start from the 0% blend, the pure new plastic. Any two blends in which more recycled content goes with lower strength show the pattern, and 25% to 50% does, so C is valid.

D.why: You may have worried that skipping the middle blends makes the comparison claim too much. The 0% and 75% blends still show strength falling as recycled content rises, which is exactly the prediction, so D completes the example.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
Some polymer coatings contain microscopic capsules of liquid resin. When a crack forms, it ruptures the capsules, and the released resin flows into the gap and hardens, restoring some of the coating's strength. Materials scientist Ines Varga tested identical coatings with and without capsules at two temperatures. Because the resin thickens in the cold, she concluded that the capsules' benefit depends strongly on temperature. For example, ______

Strength Recovered After Cracking (%)
Temperature | Without capsules | With capsules
25°C | 8 | 72
−10°C | 6 | 14
choices: coatings with capsules recovered 72% of their strength at 25°C, while coatings without capsules recovered only 8% at that temperature.
adding capsules raised strength recovery by 64 percentage points at 25°C but by only 8 percentage points at −10°C.
coatings without capsules recovered nearly the same share of their strength at both temperatures, 8% at 25°C and 6% at −10°C.
adding capsules raised strength recovery by more percentage points at −10°C than it did at 25°C.
explanation: Varga's claim is that the capsules' benefit changes with temperature, so the example has to compare the gap between the two coatings at one temperature with the gap at the other. At 25°C the capsules add 64 points (72 − 8). At −10°C they add only 8 points (14 − 6). A large benefit in warm conditions and a small one in the cold is exactly what the claim needs.

A.why: This is an accurate reading of the table, but it only shows that capsules help at 25°C. It says nothing about the cold, so it can't show that the benefit depends on temperature. You chose a true comparison that doesn't prove the passage's point.

C.why: These numbers are correct, but they describe only the coatings without capsules. The claim is about the capsules' benefit, which is the gap between the two columns. A fact about one group is not that gap.

D.why: This gets the direction backward. The gain at −10°C is 8 points and the gain at 25°C is 64 points, so the capsules help far more in the warm condition.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
stimulus: Porous pavements let rainwater pass through gaps in the surface into a bed of crushed stone underneath. The stone holds the water while it soaks slowly into the soil, so less of it runs off into storm drains. A city engineering office tested four surfaces during a heavy storm. Its report states that, in heavy storms, choosing the porous version of concrete cuts runoff more than choosing the porous version of asphalt does: ______

figure.caption: Runoff from Four Pavement Surfaces During a Heavy Storm
figure.alt: Bar graph of runoff in liters per square meter for four pavement surfaces during a heavy storm. The y-axis runs from 0 to 28 in steps of 4. There is one bar each for standard concrete, porous concrete, standard asphalt and porous asphalt.

choices: porous concrete produced the least runoff of the four surfaces, at only 4 liters per square meter.
porous concrete produced 20 fewer liters per square meter than standard concrete, while porous asphalt produced only 12 fewer than standard asphalt.
standard concrete produced 4 more liters per square meter of runoff than standard asphalt.
porous asphalt produced a larger reduction compared with standard asphalt than porous concrete produced compared with standard concrete.
explanation: The report compares two reductions: standard to porous concrete, and standard to porous asphalt. Work out both gaps. Concrete goes from 24 to 4, a reduction of 20 liters per square meter. Asphalt goes from 20 to 8, a reduction of 12. Since 20 is larger than 12, switching concrete cuts runoff more, which is the report's claim.

A.why: This is true, but it describes one bar, not a reduction. A surface can have the lowest runoff without having the largest drop from its standard version. You answered about a single value rather than the gap the statement is about.

C.why: This compares the two standard surfaces with each other. The figures are right, but the claim is about the effect of switching to porous versions, so this comparison doesn't support it.

D.why: This reverses the comparison. Asphalt drops by 12 liters per square meter and concrete drops by 20, so the concrete reduction is the larger one.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
In drypoint, an artist scratches lines into a metal plate, which raises a ridge of metal called a burr. The burr holds ink, but each pass through the press flattens it, so the lines fade from one print to the next. Etched lines are cut deeper by acid and wear more slowly. A thin electroplated layer of steel protects both kinds of line. Printmaker Tobias Wren concluded that steel facing multiplies the life of drypoint lines far more than the life of etched lines. For example, ______

Prints Made Before Visible Line Wear
Line type | Unfaced plate | Steel-faced plate
Drypoint | 20 | 180
Etched | 150 | 300
choices: steel facing added 160 prints to the life of drypoint lines and 150 prints to the life of etched lines.
steel-faced plates with etched lines yielded 300 prints, the most of any plate in the table.
steel facing let drypoint plates yield nine times as many prints, but etched plates only twice as many.
steel facing multiplied the number of prints from etched plates by more than it did for drypoint plates.
explanation: Wren's claim is about how many times longer steel facing makes the lines last, so you need ratios, not differences. Drypoint goes from 20 to 180 prints, which is 9 times as many. Etched goes from 150 to 300, which is 2 times as many. A ninefold gain against a twofold gain shows that the facing multiplies drypoint life far more.

A.why: These subtraction results are correct, but they measure the wrong kind of gap. The claim says 'multiplies', which calls for a ratio. Gains of 160 and 150 look almost equal, so this choice works against the claim instead of illustrating it.

B.why: This is an accurate reading of the table, but it picks out the largest single value instead of comparing how much facing helps each line type. The claim is about the size of the improvement, not the top count.

D.why: This reverses the comparison. Etched plates gain by a factor of 2 and drypoint plates by a factor of 9, so drypoint is multiplied by far more.
